units.title: Hello, TypeScript
units.summary: Print your first lines, store values with let and const, and add your first type annotations.

lesson.md: TypeScript is JavaScript with **types**. Before your program runs, a tool called the **type checker** reads your code and warns you about mistakes. Then the types are removed and the code runs as normal JavaScript.

lesson.code: console.log("Hello, TypeScript!");

lesson.md: `console.log` prints a value and then starts a new line. You can print several values at once: separate them with commas, and they appear with a space between them. Text goes in quotes, numbers do not, so `2 + 3` is calculated.

lesson.code:
console.log("Sum:", 2 + 3);
console.log(10 / 4);

lesson.md: A **variable** stores a value under a name. `const` creates a variable that you cannot reassign. `let` creates a variable that you can change later. Use `const` by default and `let` only when the value must change.
Strings written between backticks are **template strings**. Inside them, `${...}` inserts the value of a variable or expression into the text.

After a variable name you can write a colon and a type, for example `let age: number = 36;`. This is a **type annotation**. The three basic types are `number` for numbers, `string` for text and `boolean` for `true` or `false`.
The type checker uses annotations to find mistakes. Here `count` is a `number`, so putting the string `"five"` into it is an error. The type checker reports it before the program ever runs.

lesson.code:
let count: number = 5;
count = "five";

lesson.md: Type annotations exist only for the type checker. When the code runs, they are removed. They never change what your program prints.

card: `let age: number = 36;` is a type annotation

units.title: Basic types
units.summary: Use number, string and boolean, typed arrays and tuples, let TypeScript infer types, and compare any with unknown.

lesson.md: Every value has a type. The `typeof` operator tells you the type of a value while the program runs. It gives the name of the type as a string.
Comparisons give a `boolean`. Use `>`, `<`, `>=` and `<=` to compare numbers, `===` to test if two values are equal and `!==` to test if they are different. The `+` operator also joins strings.

lesson.output:
true
false
true false
Hello, Ada

lesson.md: If you give a variable a value right away, TypeScript works out its type for you. This is called **type inference**. Here `count` gets the type `number` without an annotation, so `count = "six"` would be an error.

An **array** is a list of values. Its type is the type of the elements followed by `[]`, for example `number[]` or `string[]`. Positions start at `0`, `length` is the number of elements and `push` adds an element at the end.
A **tuple** is an array with a fixed length where every position has its own type. `[string, number]` is a pair of a string and a number, in exactly this order.

The type `any` turns type checking off: you can do anything with the value, even mistakes. The type `unknown` also accepts every value, but you cannot use it until you check what it is. Prefer `unknown` when you do not know a type.

card: `[string, number]` is a tuple: fixed length, one type per position
`any` turns checking off, `unknown` needs a check first
`typeof x` gives the type name, e.g. `"string"`

units.title: Functions
units.summary: Write functions with typed parameters and return types, optional and default parameters, arrow functions and void.

lesson.md: A **function** is a named block of code that you can run again and again. Each parameter gets a type, and after the parentheses you write the type of the value that the function returns. `return` gives this value back.
The type checker checks every call. An argument of the wrong type, like `add("2", 3)`, is an error. A missing argument, like `add(1)`, is an error too.
A function that returns nothing has the return type `void`.
A `?` after a parameter name makes the parameter **optional**. If you leave it out, its value is `undefined`.
A parameter with `=` has a **default value**. It is used when you leave the argument out.

An **arrow function** is a short way to write a function: `(n: number) => n * 2`. You usually store it in a `const`. With one expression after `=>`, its value is returned. With curly braces, the body can have several lines and needs `return`.
TypeScript can infer the return type, but writing it helps: the type checker then also checks the code inside the function.

card: `b?: string` is optional, `b: number = 1` has a default
`(n: number) => n * 2` is an arrow function

units.title: Objects and interfaces
units.summary: Describe the shape of objects with object types, interfaces and type aliases, including optional and readonly properties.

lesson.md: An **object** groups values under names. These named values are called **properties**. You write an object in curly braces and read a property with a dot.

TypeScript infers the type `{ name: string; age: number }` for this object. You can also write an object type yourself as an annotation. Then you can change the properties, but only with values of the right type.
An `interface` gives an object type a name, so you can use it again and again. An object of this type must have all its properties. A missing property or a misspelled one is an error.
A **type alias** gives a name to any type with the keyword `type`. It works for object types and also for simple types like `string`. For objects, `interface` and `type` work almost the same.
A `?` after a property name makes the property optional: the object may leave it out. A property marked `readonly` gets its value when the object is created and cannot be changed later.
The last line is an error because `id` is `readonly`. Like all types, `readonly` is checked only by the type checker, not while the program runs.

card: `readonly id: number` cannot be changed later

units.title: Union and literal types
units.summary: Allow several types with |, narrow them with typeof and ===, and limit a value to a few exact choices with literal types.

lesson.md: A **union type** allows more than one type. `number | string` means: a number or a string. The `|` separates the choices.
With a union, you can only use what all its types have in common. `id.toUpperCase()` is an error, because `id` could be a number. You first have to check which type the value has.
An `if` statement runs a block of code only when its condition is `true`. The block after `else` runs when the condition is `false`.

Inside `if (typeof value === "string")`, TypeScript knows that `value` is a string. This is called **narrowing**. In the `else` block, it knows that `value` is a number, so you can use number methods like `toFixed(2)`, which rounds to 2 decimals.
A **literal type** is one exact value, like `"left"`. A union of literal types lists all allowed values. Calling `turn("up")` below would be an error, because `"up"` is not a `Direction`.
Comparing with `===` narrows too. After `if (s === "on")`, TypeScript knows that `s` is `"on"` inside the block, and `"off"` after it, because the function returns inside the block.

card: `number | string`: a number or a string

units.title: Working with arrays
units.summary: Transform arrays with map, filter, reduce and find, type their callbacks, and copy or combine arrays with spread.

lesson.md: Arrays have methods that take a function as an argument. This function is called a **callback**: the method calls it for every element. TypeScript knows the element type, so the parameters of the callback get their types automatically.
`map` creates a **new** array. Each element of the new array is the value that the callback returns. The original array does not change.
`filter` creates a new array with only the elements for which the callback returns `true`.

`find` returns the first element for which the callback returns `true`. If there is none, it returns `undefined`, so the type of the result is `string | undefined` here. The string method `startsWith` checks how a string begins.
`reduce` combines all elements into one value. The callback gets the result so far and the next element. The second argument of `reduce` is the start value.
You can also write the types of callback parameters and return values yourself. This is common with arrays of objects.
The **spread** syntax `...` copies all elements of an array into a new array. You can use it to copy or combine arrays.
Methods that return arrays can be chained: `nums.filter((n) => n > 4).map((n) => n * 10)` first filters, then transforms.

card: `arr.reduce((acc, x) => acc + x, 0)` combines into one value

exercises.explain: `map` calls the callback for every element and collects the squares in a new array.

`map` returns a new array. The original array stays the same.

units.title: Classes
units.summary: Build classes with fields, a constructor and methods, control access with public, private and readonly, and implement interfaces.

lesson.md: A **class** is a plan for creating objects. It lists **fields** with their types and **methods**, which are functions that belong to the object. The `constructor` runs when you create an object with `new`. Inside the class, `this` means the current object.
Every field must get a value: either directly where you declare it, like `score: number = 0;`, or in the constructor. A field without a value is an error.

Fields and methods are `public` by default: you can use them everywhere. A `private` member can only be used inside its class. A `readonly` field can only be set where it is declared or in the constructor.

Outside the class, `acc.balance` and `acc.owner = "Eve"` are errors. But `private` and `readonly` are checked only by the type checker: when the program runs, they are normal properties, and `console.log` shows them.

An interface can also list methods, like `area(): number;`. With `implements`, a class promises to have everything the interface requires. If a field or method is missing, the type checker reports an error.
A class is also a type. You can write `const p: Player = new Player("Ana");` or use `Player` as a parameter type.

card: `private`: only inside the class, `readonly`: set once
`class Square implements Shape` has all members of `Shape`

units.title: Generics
units.summary: Write reusable code with generic functions and interfaces, and use built-in generic types like Partial, Readonly and Record.

lesson.md: Sometimes a function should work with many types and still remember which one it got. `any` would lose this information. **Generics** solve this: a **type parameter** like `<T>` is a placeholder for a type that is filled in at each call.

TypeScript usually infers the type parameters from the arguments. Above, `T` is `number` in the first call and `string` in the second. You can also write them yourself after the function name. A function can have more than one type parameter.
Interfaces and type aliases can have type parameters too. `Box<number>` is a box with a number inside, and `Box<string>` is a box with a string.
You already know a generic type: arrays. `Array<number>` is another way to write `number[]`. Both mean exactly the same type.

TypeScript has useful generic types built in. `Partial<T>` makes all properties of `T` optional. `Readonly<T>` makes all of them `readonly`. `Record<K, V>` is an object with keys of type `K` and values of type `V`.
`fixed.age = 40;` would be an error here, because `fixed` has the type `Readonly<User>`.
Use generics when the type of the output depends on the type of the input. Type parameters often have short names like `T`, `K` and `V`.

card: `function first<T>(items: T[]): T` is a generic function
`interface Box<T> { value: T }` is a generic interface

exercises.explain: In `Result<number[]>`, `data` is an array of numbers. It has 3 elements.

exercises.statement: The type checker accepts this code.
exercises.code:
const config: Readonly<{ port: number }> = { port: 80 };
config.port = 8080;
exercises.explain: `Readonly` makes `port` read-only, so the second line is an error.
